section_titles.117: Annual leave with wages.- (1) Every adult worker who has completed 1

items.question: An adult worker in a private textile factory has completed 12 months of continuous service. During the year he actually worked 216 days. How many days of paid annual leave has he earned, and under which provision?
items.reference: Annual leave with wages for an adult worker accrues at one day for every 18 days of work performed during the previous 12 months (Section 117). For 216 days worked, that is 216/18 = 12 days of paid annual leave.

section_titles.115: Casual leave.- Every worker shall be entitled to casual leave for 10 (ten)
section_titles.116: Sick  leave.-  (1)  Except  a  newspaper  worker,  every  worker  shall  be

items.question: A garment worker asks how many days of casual leave and how many days of sick leave she is entitled to in a calendar year. What should HR tell her?
items.reference: A worker is entitled to 10 days of casual leave with full wages in a calendar year, which is not accumulable (Section 115), and 14 days of sick leave with full wages in a year (Section 116).

section_titles.118: Festival holidays.- (1) Every worker shall be allowed in a calendar year

items.question: Our company wants to deny festival holidays to workers who were absent the previous day. Is that allowed, and how many festival holidays are required?
items.reference: Every worker is entitled to 11 days of paid festival holidays in a calendar year; the employer fixes the dates (Section 118). Festival holidays are a statutory entitlement and cannot be denied for a prior-day absence, though a worker may be required to work on a festival holiday with substitute holiday and compensation.

section_titles.108: Extra-allowance  for  overtime.-  (1)  Where  a  worker  works  for  more

items.question: A factory worker's ordinary hourly wage is 50 taka. He worked 3 hours of overtime. How much overtime pay is he owed and under what rule?
items.reference: Overtime must be paid at twice the ordinary rate of basic wage plus dearness and ad-hoc allowances (Section 108). At an ordinary rate of 50 taka/hour, overtime is 100 taka/hour, so 3 hours = 300 taka.

section_titles.100: Daily  working  hour.-  No  adult  worker  shall  ordinarily  work  or  be
section_titles.102: Weekly working hours.- (1) No adult worker shall ordinarily work or be

items.question: What is the maximum ordinary daily and weekly working hours for an adult worker in a factory before overtime applies?
items.reference: An adult worker may ordinarily work up to 8 hours a day (Section 100) and 48 hours a week (Section 102). Work beyond this attracts overtime, and total hours including overtime should not exceed 10 hours a day, with the weekly average not exceeding 56 hours (Section 102).

section_titles.100: Daily  working  hour.-  No  adult  worker  shall  ordinarily  work  or  be
section_titles.108: Extra-allowance  for  overtime.-  (1)  Where  a  worker  works  for  more

items.manual_review: Citation corrected from s.102 (weekly hours) to s.100 (daily hours) read with s.108. Lexical support is below threshold only because the reference states the consequence - that a worker's written consent cannot waive a statutory ceiling - which is reasoning about the provision rather than wording drawn from it.
items.question: Can HR schedule an adult worker for 12 hours in a single day if the worker agrees in writing?
items.reference: No. Section 100 fixes the daily ceiling: an adult worker shall not ordinarily work more than 8 hours in a day, and even with overtime under Section 108 the worker may work up to 10 hours in a day. A written agreement by the worker cannot override that statutory ceiling, so 12 hours in a single day is not permitted.

section_titles.26: Termination of employment of worker by an employer otherwise than
section_titles.27: Termination of employment by workers.- (1) A permanent worker may

items.question: A permanent monthly-rated worker is being terminated by the employer through simple notice (not for misconduct). What notice period or pay in lieu applies?
items.reference: For termination of a permanent worker by the employer through notice, a monthly-rated worker must be given 120 days' written notice, or wages in lieu of that notice (Section 26). The worker is also entitled to compensation of 30 days' wages for every completed year of service (or gratuity, whichever is higher).

section_titles.20: Retrenchment.-  (1)  Any  worker  may  be  retrenched  from  service  of  any

items.question: Our company must reduce headcount due to genuine redundancy. What is the process and compensation for retrenchment of a worker with 5 years of service?
items.reference: Retrenchment of a worker who has been in continuous service for at least one year requires one month's written notice (or pay in lieu) stating reasons, notice to the Chief Inspector, and compensation of 30 days' wages for every completed year of service (Section 20). For 5 years' service that is 150 days' wages, and 'last in, first out' ordinarily applies (Section 20).

section_titles.123: Time  of payment  of wages.-  (1)  The  wages  of  a  worker  shall be  paid

items.question: By what date must wages be paid to workers, and who is responsible for timely payment?
items.reference: Wages must be paid before the expiry of the 7th working day after the end of the wage period for which they are payable (Section 123). The employer (or a person designated by the employer) is responsible for the timely payment of wages.

section_titles.125: Deductions  which  may  be  made  from  wages.-  (1)  Except  the  cases
section_titles.126: Deductions from wages for absence from duty.- (1) Deductions from

items.question: An employer wants to deduct the cost of a damaged machine from a worker's wages. Is that a lawful deduction?
items.reference: Deductions from wages are only permitted on the grounds specified in the Act (Section 125). A deduction for damage to or loss of goods or money entrusted to the worker is allowed only where the damage or loss is directly attributable to the worker's neglect or default, and only after the worker has been given an opportunity to show cause; the deduction cannot exceed the value of the damage (Section 126).

section_titles.123: Time  of payment  of wages.-  (1)  The  wages  of  a  worker  shall be  paid

items.question: When a worker's employment ends, within how many days must all wages due be paid?
items.reference: Where a worker's employment is terminated (by retirement, dismissal, retrenchment, discharge or otherwise), all wages payable to the worker must be paid within 30 working days of the termination (Section 123(2)).

section_titles.46: Right  to  maternity  benefit  and  liability  for  its  payment.-  (1)  Every
section_titles.48: Amount of maternity benefit.- (1) The maternity benefit which is payable

items.question: A pregnant employee has worked for our company for 7 months. She asks about her maternity benefit and leave. What is she entitled to?
items.reference: A woman who has worked for the employer for at least 6 months preceding her delivery is entitled to maternity benefit for 16 weeks total — 8 weeks preceding the expected delivery and 8 weeks immediately following delivery (Section 46). Maternity benefit is payable at the rate of her average daily/weekly/monthly wages (Section 48).

section_titles.50: Restrictions  on  termination  of  employment  of  a  woman  in  certain

items.question: Can we terminate a woman worker while she is on maternity leave, citing restructuring?
items.reference: No. It is unlawful for an employer to dismiss or terminate a woman worker during the period of her maternity leave, or to give notice of dismissal such that it expires during that period, without sufficient cause; doing so also forfeits the employer's ability to withhold maternity benefit (Section 50). Restructuring is not sufficient cause to remove protection of maternity benefit.

section_titles.46: Right  to  maternity  benefit  and  liability  for  its  payment.-  (1)  Every

items.question: A woman worker had two surviving children at the time she applied for maternity benefit for a third child. Is she eligible for cash maternity benefit?
items.reference: Maternity benefit (cash payment) is not payable to a woman who, at the time of her delivery, already has two or more surviving children, though she remains entitled to the leave itself (Section 46(2)). She may take the maternity leave but the cash maternity benefit is not payable in that circumstance.

section_titles.23: Punishment  for  misconduct  and  conviction.-  (1)  Notwithstanding
section_titles.24: Procedure of punishment.- (1) No order of punishment under section 23

items.question: A worker is accused of theft at the workplace. Can we dismiss him immediately, or is a procedure required?
items.reference: A worker may be dismissed for misconduct such as theft, but only after a proper procedure: a written charge, an opportunity to explain, and a formal inquiry in which the worker can defend himself (Section 24). Dismissal for misconduct without following this procedure is unlawful. Theft is listed among acts constituting misconduct (Section 23).

section_titles.24: Procedure of punishment.- (1) No order of punishment under section 23

items.question: During a disciplinary inquiry, can the employer suspend the worker, and for how long, and what payment applies?
items.reference: Yes. Pending an inquiry into misconduct, the employer may suspend the worker; the period of such suspension must not ordinarily exceed 60 days (Section 24). During suspension the worker is entitled to a subsistence allowance equal to half of his average wages (Section 24).

section_titles.23: Punishment  for  misconduct  and  conviction.-  (1)  Notwithstanding

items.question: What punishments other than dismissal can an employer impose on a worker found guilty of misconduct after inquiry?
items.reference: Instead of dismissal, an employer may impose lesser punishments such as removal, reduction to a lower post, stoppage of promotion, withholding of increment, fine, suspension without wages, or censure/warning, depending on the gravity of the misconduct (Section 23). The punishment must follow a valid inquiry.

section_titles.4: Classification of workers and probation period.- (1) Workers employed

items.question: We hired a worker for a clerical role. How long can the probation period last before he becomes permanent?
items.reference: For a worker whose function is of a clerical nature, the probationary period is 6 months. For other (non-clerical) workers it is 3 months, which may be extended by a further 3 months. On satisfactory completion of probation the worker is confirmed as permanent (Section 4).

section_titles.4: Classification of workers and probation period.- (1) Workers employed

items.question: Can an employer extend the probation of a non-clerical worker beyond the initial period, and by how much?
items.reference: Yes. For a non-clerical worker the initial probation period is 3 months, and it may be extended by an additional 3 months where the employer cannot assess the worker's performance within the first period (Section 4). If the worker continues to be employed after the probationary period without confirmation, he is deemed to be a permanent worker.

section_titles.92: Canteen.-  (1)  In  an  establishment  where  more  than  100  (one  hundred)
section_titles.94: Rooms for children.- (1) In every establishment, where 40 (forty) or more

items.question: At what number of workers does a factory become legally required to provide certain welfare facilities such as a canteen and a childcare room?
items.reference: Under the Act, a canteen must be provided where 100 or more workers are ordinarily employed (Section 92). A room for children (childcare/creche) must be provided where 40 or more women workers are employed (Section 94). These are welfare requirements under Chapter VIII.

section_titles.63: Fencing  of  machinery.-  (1)  In  every  establishment  the  following

items.question: A worker was injured because a dangerous machine part was not fenced. What does the Act require regarding fencing of machinery?
items.reference: Section 63 requires that the specified dangerous machinery, while in motion or in use, be securely fenced by safeguards of substantial construction, and that the fencing be kept in position while the part is in motion or in use. This covers moving parts of prime movers and fly wheels, water wheels and turbines, projecting stock-bars, and transmission machinery unless it is so positioned or constructed as to be equally safe.

section_titles.99: Introduction of compulsory group insurance.- (1) In  an establishment

items.question: Is the employer required to insure workers against workplace injury, and from what number of workers?
items.reference: The Act provides for compulsory group insurance in establishments where a minimum number of workers (100 or more permanent workers) are employed, to cover death and injury (Section 99). This is in addition to the employer's liability to pay compensation for employment injury under Chapter XII.

section_titles.150: Liability  of  the  employer  to  pay  compensation.-  (1)  If  a  worker  is

items.question: A worker died in a workplace accident arising out of and in the course of employment. Is the employer liable to pay compensation, and under what provision?
items.reference: Yes. An employer is liable to pay compensation where personal injury or death is caused to a worker by an accident arising out of and in the course of his employment (Section 150). The amount for death is fixed by the Act's schedule, and the claim is dealt with under Chapter XII.

section_titles.2: Definitions.- In this Act, unless there  is anything repugnant in the  subject

items.question: How many years of continuous service qualify a worker for gratuity, and how is it calculated?
items.reference: Gratuity is payable to a worker who has completed at least one year of continuous service, calculated as wages of 30 days for every completed year of service (or any part in excess of six months), based on the wages last drawn (Section 2(10) definition of gratuity, applied on termination/retirement). For workers with longer service the rate may be higher under applicable rules.

section_titles.34: Restrictions on employment of children and adolescents.- (1) No child

items.question: A contractor wants to employ a 13-year-old in our factory. Is that permitted?
items.reference: No. No child (a person who has not completed 14 years of age) may be employed or permitted to work in any occupation or establishment (Section 34). An adolescent (14 to under 18) may work only subject to restrictions and with a certificate of fitness (Sections 34-44).

section_titles.179: Requirements  for  registration.-  (1)  A  trade  union  shall not  be  entitled

items.question: A group of workers wants to form a trade union. What is the minimum membership requirement for registration?
items.reference: A trade union of workers in an establishment may apply for registration; it generally must have a minimum membership of a prescribed proportion of the total workers (20% of the total number of workers) to be registered, and no union with fewer than the required members can be registered (Section 179). Registration is granted by the Registrar of Trade Unions.

section_titles.202: Collective bargaining agent.- (1) Where there is only one trade union in

items.question: Where there are several registered unions in one establishment, how is the collective bargaining agent determined?
items.reference: Where there is more than one registered trade union in an establishment, the collective bargaining agent (CBA) is determined by the Registrar through a secret ballot, and the union receiving the highest number of votes (not less than one-third of the total workers) is certified as the CBA (Section 202).

section_titles.103: Weekly holiday.- Every worker employed in an establishment-

items.question: Is a weekly holiday mandatory for factory workers, and is it paid?
items.reference: Yes. An adult worker in a factory is entitled to one day of weekly holiday, and it is a paid holiday; wages cannot be deducted for the weekly holiday (Section 103). If a worker is required to work on the weekly holiday, a substitute holiday must be provided.

section_titles.101: Interval for rest or meal.- In an establishment no worker shall be liable

items.question: How many hours can an adult worker work continuously before being entitled to a rest interval?
items.reference: An adult worker cannot be required to work for more than 6 hours in a day without a rest or meal interval of at least one hour, or more than 5 hours without an interval of at least half an hour (Section 101). Total spread-over of work in a day, including intervals, should not exceed the limit set by the Act.

section_titles.27: Termination of employment by workers.- (1) A permanent worker may
section_titles.26: Termination of employment of worker by an employer otherwise than

items.question: Is a worker who resigns entitled to any benefit, and what notice must the worker give?
items.reference: A permanent worker who wishes to resign must give 60 days' written notice to the employer (Section 27). On resignation after at least 5 years of continuous service, the worker is entitled to compensation/gratuity as provided (Section 27 read with Section 26), typically 14 days' wages for each completed year of service for resignation, depending on length of service.

section_titles.117: Annual leave with wages.- (1) Every adult worker who has completed 1

items.question: Can unused annual leave be carried forward or encashed?
items.reference: Un-availed annual leave with wages may be accumulated up to a limit (for adults, up to 40 days), and a worker who is refused leave or whose service ends is entitled to be paid wages in lieu of the un-availed annual leave (Section 117). Accumulation beyond the statutory ceiling lapses.

section_titles.138: Establishment  of  the  Minimum  Wages  Board.-  (1)  The  Government
section_titles.139: Recommendation  of  minimum  rates  of wages  for  certain  workers.-
section_titles.140: Power  to  declare  minimum  rate  of  wages.-  (1)  Upon  receipt  of  the

items.question: What is the minimum wage mechanism under the Act — who fixes minimum wages?
items.reference: Minimum rates of wages for workers are recommended by the Minimum Wages Board constituted by the Government, and the Government declares minimum wages by notification in the official Gazette for different industries or classes of workers (Sections 138-140). Paying below the declared minimum wage is an offence.

section_titles.108: Extra-allowance  for  overtime.-  (1)  Where  a  worker  works  for  more

items.question: Must an employer keep a record of overtime worked, and where?
items.reference: Section 108(3) provides that, for ensuring compliance with the overtime provisions, the Government may by rules prescribe the register to be maintained by the employer. The Act itself therefore does not set out the register's form; the specific record-keeping obligation is fixed by the rules made under this section.

section_titles.23: Punishment  for  misconduct  and  conviction.-  (1)  Notwithstanding
section_titles.24: Procedure of punishment.- (1) No order of punishment under section 23

items.question: A worker was absent without leave for 12 consecutive days. Can this be treated as misconduct or abandonment?
items.reference: Habitual absence without leave, or absence without leave for more than 10 days, is listed as misconduct (Section 23). The employer must still follow the inquiry procedure — issue a notice/charge, give the worker an opportunity to explain, and hold an inquiry — before imposing any punishment (Section 24).

section_titles.45: Prohibition  of  engagement  of  women  worker  in  work  in  certain

items.question: Can we assign heavy or arduous work to a pregnant worker in the weeks before her delivery?
items.reference: No. An employer must not knowingly employ a woman in any establishment during the 8 weeks immediately following the day of her delivery, and must not require a pregnant woman to do work that is arduous, involves long hours of standing, or is likely to interfere with her pregnancy in the period preceding delivery (Section 45).

section_titles.89: First-aid  appliances.-  (1)  In  every  establishment  the  first-aid  box  or

items.question: Is the employer required to provide first-aid facilities, and at what worker count must a dispensary/medical facility be provided?
items.reference: First-aid boxes or cupboards must be provided and maintained in every establishment, at a rate of at least one for every 150 workers (Section 89). Where 300 or more workers are employed, a dispensary/medical room with prescribed medical staff and equipment must be maintained (Section 89).

section_titles.232: Application of the Chapter.- (1) This Chapter shall apply to a company
section_titles.234: Establishment  of  Participation  Fund  and  Welfare  Fund.-  (1)  Every

items.question: Are workers entitled to any annual bonus or profit participation under the Act?
items.reference: In establishments to which Chapter XV applies (companies with a certain paid-up capital or fixed assets), workers are entitled to participate in the company's profits through a Workers' Participation Fund and Welfare Fund, with a prescribed percentage (5%) of net profit allocated (Sections 232-234). This is separate from festival bonus, which is governed by rules and practice.

section_titles.22: Discharge  from  service.-  (1) A  worker  may be  discharged  from  service
section_titles.23: Punishment  for  misconduct  and  conviction.-  (1)  Notwithstanding
section_titles.26: Termination of employment of worker by an employer otherwise than

items.question: What is the difference between 'termination', 'dismissal', and 'discharge' of a worker under the Act?
items.reference: Termination (Section 26) is ending employment by notice or pay in lieu without alleging misconduct. Dismissal (Section 23) is removal for proven misconduct after inquiry, and may be without notice. Discharge (Section 22) is ending employment on grounds of physical or mental incapacity or continued ill-health, certified by a registered medical practitioner. Each carries different notice and compensation consequences.
